iOS for Android developers · Puzzle 2 · 3 of 5

Queues, not handlers

On Android, you post work to the main thread with a Handler and run slow work on another thread or a coroutine on another thread. iOS has one system for both. Here it is.

Builds on: open one to see the idea this puzzle uses.

  • Puzzle 1: The run loop is your Looper

    Any iOS thread can have a run loop, and the main thread always does: an event loop that handles work when there is some and puts the thread to sleep when there is none. The app framework starts the main thread's run loop for you, just as Android starts the main Looper. UI work belongs on that loop, so blocking it freezes the screen.

Starting from zero? The blocks under this puzzle are 2 puzzles: 0 → 1. Know them already? Start here.

The problem

In puzzle 1, slow work on the main run loop froze the screen. On Android you'd move it to another thread, a coroutine on Dispatchers.IO for example, and then post the result back to the main thread with a Handler. On iOS you don't create those threads yourself either. Where does the slow work go, and how does the result get back?

See it

Save this diagram as a GIF

The building block

iOS's answer is GCD, Grand Central Dispatch. Instead of threads, you think in dispatch queues: first-in, first-out lines of tasks. You add a task, a closure (a block of code you pass around, like a Kotlin lambda), to a queue; GCD runs it on one of a pool of threads that it creates and manages for you.

A queue is either serial, running one task at a time in order, or concurrent, able to run several of its tasks at the same time on different threads.

One queue is special: the main queue. It's serial, and its tasks run on the main thread: they're one of the kinds of work the main run loop from puzzle 1 picks up, next to touches and timers. The others you'll use most are the global queues: concurrent queues GCD provides, ready to use, for work off the main thread. So the iOS pattern is the Android one, with new names:

DispatchQueue.global().async {          // a concurrent queue: off the main thread
    let image = loadBigImage()          // slow work
    DispatchQueue.main.async {          // back to the main queue
        imageView.image = image         // screen work, on the main thread
    }
}

DispatchQueue.main.async is iOS's handler.post: it adds your task to the main queue, and the main thread runs it when it gets there. The rule is the same as Android's: screen work only on the main queue.

The analogy

The clerk from puzzle 1 still has one in-tray: the main queue. But the back office no longer has named workers: it has more in-trays, and a manager (GCD) who assigns whoever is free to pick up the next task.

Check yourself

You add three tasks to a serial queue, one after another. How do they run?

Right. Serial: one at a time, in order.

Not quite. A serial queue keeps the order: first in, first out.

Not quite. That's a concurrent queue; a serial one runs one task at a time.

Why does the image go back through DispatchQueue.main.async before it's shown?

Not quite. Size isn't the issue: only the main thread may touch the screen.

Right. Screen work belongs on the main queue.

Not quite. Nothing is deleted; the result has to be used on the main thread.

What's the difference between a dispatch queue and a thread?

Not quite. Only the main queue is tied to the main thread; other queues use GCD's pool.

Not quite. A concurrent queue can run tasks on several threads; queues and threads aren't one-to-one.

Right. Tasks wait in queues; threads run them.

Sources

  • Apple: DispatchQueue ("An object that manages the execution of tasks serially or concurrently on your app's main thread or on a background thread. Dispatch queues are FIFO queues to which your application can submit tasks in the form of block objects. Dispatch queues execute tasks either serially or concurrently. Work submitted to dispatch queues executes on a pool of threads managed by the system.")

What you now know

Grand Central Dispatch runs tasks from dispatch queues on a pool of threads it manages. A serial queue runs one task at a time, in order; a concurrent queue can run several at once. The main queue runs on the main thread, so DispatchQueue.main.async is iOS's handler.post.
